description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

schema.description:

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to [REDACTED_EMAIL]' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

This server helps users set up and manage their Shopify stores.

## Starting a New Business
Users who are still shaping a business can work on it here before they have a store. None of these tools needs one.
- Naming: generate-business-names suggests business names from a short description of what the user sells, who it is for, or the feeling they want.

When the user settles on a name, offer to check domains for it.
Never present a domain as available unless generate-domain-names checked it; a domain you suggest yourself may already be taken.
Follow the user's lead rather than walking them through every step.

## Store Creation
Users who don't have a store yet can use get-new-store-previews to create one from a short description.
After calling get-new-store-previews, encourage the user to browse the previews and pick the theme they like best.
Each preview has a signup link — signing up through it creates a real Shopify store with that theme and matching products pre-installed.
Encourage continued brainstorming: users can try different descriptions, tweak ideas, or explore new directions without commitment.

- Customers: list and search customers.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. # event-intelligence

Sourced event facts and research cache.

## Implementation status

This repository contains an internal, bounded HTTP(S) retrieval utility under `src/security/`, a content privacy boundary and tenant-scoped flows under `src/privacy/`, deterministic local DNS/HTTP/TLS and privacy fixtures, a Node 22 test runner, and compile-checked consumer declarations. Retrieval validates URL and DNS policy, pins connections to vetted addresses, revalidates redirects, bounds response resources, and rejects unsupported or mismatched media. Privacy flows keep untrusted content quarantined until a configured trusted review approves the public facts.

The utility is not yet integrated with the accepted research request/response contract. EI-01 (#7) and EI-09 (#9) remain prerequisites. Event source discovery, factual extraction, provenance, caching, provider connections, downstream parser hardening, and live release evidence remain pending. The local socket fixtures measure their own requests only; they do not assert production or external egress telemetry.

Run `npm ci`, `make verify CASE=safe-retrieval MODE=mock`, `make verify CASE=content-privacy MODE=mock`, `make verify CASE=eval-policy-unit MODE=unit`, `npm run test:runner`, and `npm run typecheck` with Node 22.23.3 and Python 3.9 or newer (CI pins Python 3.11.17). The Python route emits the actual Python runtime and expected, executed, passed, failed, skipped-case, and total skip-event counts; it separately identifies subtest and setup/teardown hook skips and errors. It fails when no tests execute or any case fails, any skip event occurs, or any test unexpectedly succeeds. It covers local policy and runner unit tests only; it is not the held-out benchmark or evidence that the policy is promotion-ready. The reserved Node `CASE=evals MODE=mock` route remains fail-closed until a benchmark suite is implemented. Details and limits are in [controlled retrieval](docs/security/controlled-retri

=================== PeytonLi__Conduit README
# Conduit

Conduit is a planned supplier delay recovery agent. It connects supplier messages with purchase orders, inventory, and dated demand to identify shortages, investigate alternatives, collect quotes, and prepare a recovery plan for business owner approval.

The proposed workflow supports email and supplier calls using DeepSeek, ElevenLabs, and SignalWire, with neatlogs for runtime traces, Entire for development history, and CFO.ai for the product's business model.

**Status:** The Phase 1 application and local-development foundation has passed local verification. No live provider or supplier workflow is enabled, and Phase 2 business behavior remains unimplemented. See [BUILD_STATUS.md](BUILD_STATUS.md) for evidence and remaining gates.

Start with the [product requirements](PRD.md). Implementation agents should read the [compact handoff](AGENT_HANDOFF.md) and [current build status](BUILD_STATUS.md), then load the relevant [reference chapters](docs/prd/). The [research notes](research/neathack-research.md) cover hackathon requirements, precedents, and integration research.

The current milestone and verification evidence are tracked in [BUILD_STATUS.md](BUILD_STATUS.md). The scaffold intentionally leaves Phase 2 business behavior unimplemented.

## Local development

### Prerequisites

- Node.js 22
- pnpm 10.34.6
- Docker running locally (required by Supabase CLI)
- Playwright Chromium for browser tests

### Start the app

```sh
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm db:start
pnpm db:reset
pnpm exec supabase status -o env
```

Copy the local `API_URL`, `ANON_KEY`, and `SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` from the status output into `.env.local` as `SUPABASE_URL`, `SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY`, and `SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY`. Do not commit `.env.local`; the publishable key is for local development and the secret key must stay server-side.

```sh
pnpm seed:demo
pnpm dev
```

`pnpm seed:demo` creates the local demo accounts `[REDACTED_EMAIL]`, `[REDACTED_EMAIL]`, `[REDACTED_EMAIL]`, and `[REDACTED_EMAIL]`. Their shared password is `HarborPackLocalOnly!2026`; it is intentionally local-only and must never be reused for a real account.

### Checks

```sh
pnpm lint
pnpm typecheck
pnpm test
pnpm db:reset
pnpm test:db
pnpm exec playwright install chromium
pnpm test:e2e
pnpm build
```

`pnpm db:reset` applies migrations and loads the two-organization local seed. The integration tests connect only to the local Supabase database.

# TeamLoop

**A crew of AI bots that runs your laptop.** Chat with the lead bot, S, from the desktop app, your
phone or Telegram. S plans the job and hands steps to specialist bots. They really control the
computer (apps, windows, settings, any app's screen, their own logged-in Chrome), check their own
work, and ask you before anything risky. Free models only, and with a neatlogs key every step is traced in neatlogs.

Built for **neatHack** (Oct 10–12, 2026) by @sourabhnirvani and @JrKrishh. It is a fresh rebuild of
our earlier private project, Agent S: same ideas, and all code here was written during the event.

- Plan and work split: [PLAN.md](PLAN.md)
- Teammate setup: [HANDOFF.md](HANDOFF.md)
- Start here: [below](#start-here)

## Start here

Windows 10/11, Python 3.11+, Node 20+. Everything below is free.

```
git clone https://github.com/sourabhnirvani/teamloop
cd teamloop
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
copy .env.example .env          # add at least one free key (see below)
cd ui && npm ci && npm run build && cd ..
python -m teamloop              # open http://127.0.0.1:8790
```

**Keys.** Use free-tier keys from accounts with no card attached: Gemini (aistudio.google.com),
Groq, NVIDIA (build.nvidia.com), OpenRouter `:free` models, z.ai flash, or local Ollama with no key.
Put them in `.env`, or paste them into Settings → API keys (pasted keys are checked, then locked in the
key vault and never shown again). "check models" in any chat tells you which ones answer.

**Ways to use it**

| | How |
|---|---|
| Desktop app | `cd desktop && npm install && npm start` (or `npm run dist` for a portable `TeamLoop.exe`). Runs in the tray; Quit stops the crew. See [desktop/README.md](desktop/README.md). |
| No Electron | double-click `start_teamloop.vbs` (hidden server + browser) or `start_teamloop.bat` |
| Phone | Settings → Phone → Pair a phone, scan the QR. Free Cloudflare tunnel, needs `cloudflared` (`winget install Cloudflare.cloudflared`). The link changes each time the server restarts. |
| Telegram | make a bot with @BotFather, put `TELEGRAM_TOKEN` in `.env`, message the bot once, put the id it sends you in `TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID` (comma-separated for more people), restart |
| Terminal | `python -m teamloop.cli "battery?"`, or `python -m teamloop.cli` to chat (`--chat dm-desk` for one bot) |
| Evals | `python -m evals.run` (no model calls) or `python -m evals.run --live`; results in `evidence/evals/` |
| Tests | `python -m pytest` |

**Try:** "open calculator", "volume 30", "@desk what apps are open?", "Scout, search free LLM APIs for
students", "save a note on the Desktop: hello", "every Monday at 9am remind me to check the report",
"remember I like short answers", "stop". The demo goal: *"Research the top 3 free LLM APIs for students,
write a short report on the Desktop, open it, and remind me about it every Monday."*

**Safety.** Anything that acts as you (closing apps, deleting, sending, buying, locking, shutting down)
shows an approval card first; no answer in 2 minutes means no, and after a "no" the same request isn't asked again in that chat for
10 minutes (say "ask me again"). Bots never
touch a window titled "TeamLoop". Through the phone tunnel, every `/api` call needs a paired phone.


=================== haodaz__hioffer README
# hioffer

A PhD-application agent, built in public for neatHack (Oct 10-12, 2026).

**Live demo:** https://hioffer-one.vercel.app (frontend) · API: https://hioffer-production.up.railway.app · Demo applicant is fictional.

Give it one goal, e.g. *"prepare my applications to these 3 CS PhD programs"*, and it:

1. Builds a **material library** from the applicant's files (CV, SOP, research statement, writing samples, recommenders).
2. Researches each program's **official requirements** (deadlines, word limits, documents, letters, fee), keeping the source URL and quoted text for every fact.
3. Finds **faculty whose recent work matches** the applicant's interests (department pages + OpenAlex), keeps only papers OpenAlex actually returned, flags whether they appear to take students, and adds light **co-author / alumni links** to the applicant's circle.
4. **Tailors materials** per program (fit paragraph per advisor, SOP variant within limits) and drafts outreach emails, every sentence tagged with its source.
5. **Verifies its own output** (word limits, citations resolve, claims supported, requirement coverage), revises what the writer can fix, turns the rest into to-dos, and checkpoints every step so a crashed run resumes.

The human sends emails, pays fees and submits. The agent never does.

## Architecture

```
web/ (Next.js)  ──SSE──▶  hioffer/server.py (FastAPI)
                              │  chat.py: root agent, talks + emits cards
                              ▼
                 orchestrator.py  (WORKFLOW span, JSON checkpoints in workspace/)
     librarian → program_researcher → advisor_scout → connector → writer → verifier
       AGENT         AGENT + TOOLs        AGENT + TOOLs    AGENT    AGENT   GUARDRAIL
                     fetch_page       fetch_page, find_author, recent_works (OpenAlex)
```

Every run is one neatlogs trace: the workflow span, one AGENT span per sub-agent, one TOOL span per
tool call, plus a CHAIN span when malformed JSON has to be repaired.

## Hackathon tooling

- **neatlogs** traces every agent run (model/tool calls, tokens, cost). Runs are tagged (`run1` … `run5`,
  `after-fix`, `pruned`) so before/after comparisons are one filter away.
- **Entire** records the coding-agent sessions behind each commit (`entire checkpoint list`).
- **cfo.ai** holds the business plan (pricing, costs, revenue, runway), fed by the per-run cost in neatlogs: https://cfo.ai/s/A_qiW6hIGmm-3fDR

See [hackathon.md](hackathon.md) for the dated build log, the failures found in traces and their fixes.

## Setup

Requires Python 3.10+ (we use [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)) and Node 20+.

```bash
cp .env.example .env          # fill in LITELLM_*, NEATLOGS_API_KEY, OPENALEX_API_KEY
uv sync                       # Python deps into .venv
cd web && npm install && cd ..
```

## Run

Command line, full pipeline for the demo applicant (fictional; see `examples/applicants/priya/README.md`):

```bash
uv run python -m hioffer.cli run examples/applicants/priya --program Washington --tag my-run
```

Outputs land in `workspace/priya/<program>/` (`requirements.json`, `advisors_connected.json`,
`materials_vN.json`, `verification_vN.json`, `final.json`). Re-running skips finished steps.

Web app:

```bash
uv run uvicorn hioffer.server:app --port 8000 --reload
cd web && npm run dev          # then open http://localhost:3000
```

## Tests

```bash
NEATLOGS_API_KEY=x uv run pytest -q
```

Covers the deterministic parts: JSON parsing, tool-result pruning, citation tags, offer scoring, to-do
merging and program-list merging. The model-driven stages are checked by the verifier at runtime and by
the neatlogs traces.

## Evidence

- `evidence/neatlogs/` — trace list, trace tree, detections, the run-1 error inside the trace.
- `evidence/entire/` — `entire checkpoint list`, `checkpoint explain`, `checkpoint tokens`, `entire why`.
- `evidence/cfo-ai/` — the financial model pages; public link above.
- `evidence/2026-10-10-run*/` — raw agent outputs before and after each fix.

## Limitations

- Faculty discovery depends on department pages being fetchable and on OpenAlex author disambiguation;
  faculty whose record cannot be matched are listed under "skipped" rather than guessed.
- Requirements come only from pages the researcher could fetch; anything not found is listed as not found.
- One applicant per workspace; no accounts.

# PreJudge: get roasted before the judges do

Paste a public GitHub repo. An AI judge checks it against the neatHack rubric, verifies README
claims against the code (with file:line evidence), and returns a score, a fix list ordered by
points and a roast. It never runs the audited code. Built for neatHack (Oct 10–12, 2026).

- `backend/`: FastAPI, Groq agent, deterministic scoring, neatlogs tracing (`python -m app.cli <repo_url> --full`)
- `frontend/`: React + Vite + TypeScript UI (see [frontend/README.md](frontend/README.md))
- [EVIDENCE.md](EVIDENCE.md): traces, before/after numbers, throughput, hackathon evidence

## Business plan

PreJudge is bootstrapped, sold as monthly licenses ($199 / $499 / $999) and pay-per-event audits
($49 / $149), with a free tier for individual teams. AI costs $0.0095 per audit (measured in our
traces). In the Main scenario it's profitable every month from Feb 2027, with a 97% gross margin,
and never runs out of cash.

- Summary: [docs/business-plan.md](docs/business-plan.md) (pricing, costs, scenarios, v1 → v3
  changes, risks, hiring rule)

=================== AdiGoCrazy__atlas-commerce README
# Atlas Commerce

Atlas Commerce is a prototype for assessing candidate regions, ranking products for seeded active regions, and proposing bounded profile changes from synthetic signals. The demo uses fictional regions and simulated commerce results; it is not a production commerce system. Candidate approval, autonomous execution, evaluation, and rollback are not yet wired into the dashboard.

## How it works

1. An operator submits a candidate region; the app stores it and a simulated finance assessment in SQLite.
2. The dashboard displays local base/growth/downside results and may display a validated, operator-supplied cfo.ai export. No live cfo.ai MCP read is implemented.
3. The dashboard previews rankings for seeded regions with active profiles. It does not approve candidates or run the autonomous worker.
4. Application services can normalize fixture signals and propose bounded profile changes, but activation/evaluation/rollback are not connected as an end-to-end UI workflow.

The planned product includes human approval, autonomous updates, and rollback. Those controls are not present in the current demo.

## Architecture

The planned implementation is a Python modular monolith: Streamlit presentation calls application services; domain, ranking, and integration logic stay outside the UI. SQLite stores durable state and immutable recommendation versions. External services are accessed through small adapters and must expose clear success, degraded, or failed status.

```text
Streamlit dashboard → application services → region lifecycle / finance
                   → autonomous worker → signals → policy checks
                                         → candidate ranking → evaluation
                                         → activate or reject
                   → recommendation service → storefront preview
                   → SQLite state/version history

neatlogs: runtime traces and evaluations
Entire: development context and checkpoints
cfo.ai: financial model and regional scenarios
```

The main domain concepts are `Region`, `RegionProfile`, `Product`, `Signal`, `EventWindow`, `FinanceAssessment`, `RecommendationVersion`, `RecommendationItem`, `UpdateCycle`, and `EvidenceReference`. SQLite is the prototype source of truth; activation and rollback must be transactional.

## Recommendation and safety rules

The initial ranker is deterministic and explainable:

```text
score = base popularity + regional interest match + temporary event boost
        + margin bonus - policy penalty
```

LLMs may extract or translate signals and explain decisions, but they do not choose final ranking scores. Weight changes are bounded, versioned, and reversible. Work is idempotent by source/region/event/cycle identifiers; stale or low-confidence signals do not trigger updates, and temporary event boosts expire.

# Migration Parachute

A schema migration can be correct and still take down a service. Migration Parachute is an agent that runs an expand / backfill / contract migration on a live Postgres table. When another session holds the rows it needs, it rolls back the chunk, records who holds the lock, shrinks its batch, waits, and resumes from a saved cursor. It will not prepare the destructive step until a deterministic verifier proves parity, and it will not run that step until an owner approves the exact SQL.

**Demo:** [179-second execution UI recording](https://github.com/Sher110106/migration-parachute/releases/download/v0.1.0/execution-ui-replay.mp4) · [release notes](https://github.com/Sher110106/migration-parachute/releases/tag/v0.1.0)

Built for neatHack 2026 (10–12 October 2026). All code in this repository was written during the event.

> The demo runs on a **fictional local fixture**: 2,000 customers and 10,000 orders on local Postgres 15, emails on the reserved `.test` domain. It never touches a real database.

## Results

Same fixture, same seeded fault: a separate session holds row locks on keys 4,001–4,100 for 6 seconds while the backfill reaches them. The per-statement lock budget is 300 ms.

| Run | Outcome | Retries | Lock wait | Rows kept |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Baseline: one `UPDATE` in one transaction | `FAILED`, whole transaction rolled back | – | 452 ms | 0 |
| Agent with first recovery policy (`naive-retry/v0`: same batch, 50 ms wait) | `PAUSED_LOCK_BUDGET`, retry budget spent | 6 | 2,647 ms | 4,000 |
| Agent with fixed recovery policy (`adaptive/v1`) | parity proven, `CONTRACT_READY` | 4 | 1,817 ms | 10,000 |

| Agent with a language-model planner (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash via OpenRouter, inside the same policy fence) | parity proven, `CONTRACT_READY` | 2 | 751 ms | 10,000 |

Neither failing run claims success. Full replay suite, 12 scenarios: v0 passes 11, v1 passes 12. Both have zero false successes and zero destructive statements run without approval. Raw records: [`evidence/replay-naive-v0.json`](evidence/replay-naive-v0.json) and [`evidence/replay-adaptive-v1.json`](evidence/replay-adaptive-v1.json). Lock-wait figures vary by tens of milliseconds between runs; three repeats of each policy gave the same outcome every time.

The language-model planner passes all 12 scenarios with no rejected decisions: 14 decisions, 9,278 input and 5,239 output tokens, $0.0094 in total ([`evidence/replay-llm-deepseek-v4.1-flash.json`](evidence/replay-llm-deepseek-v4.1-flash.json)). On the lock run it read the blocker's age from the error evidence: after the first timeout it waited 1 s; when the blocking transaction was 4.1 s old it waited 3 s, so it needed two retries where the fixed policy needed four. Each answer must name one of the actions policy allows, inside its bounds; anything else is rejected and recorded, and the determ

The v0 policy was committed and measured before the fix. The git history shows the order: `ed9edbe` (v0, 11/12) then `5e05e92` (fix, 12/12). The records each commit produced at the time are kept in [`evidence/history/`](evidence/history/); they used a 3.0 s lock. The lock is now held for 6 s, because v1's blocker inspection made each failed attempt slower, and at 3.5 s the naive policy sometimes outlasted the lock.

## What the agent does

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  spec[MigrationSpec] --> orch[Orchestrator]
  orch -->|observation + allowed options| planner[Planner: Claude or deterministic]
  planner -->|one action| guard[Policy guard]
  guard -->|typed tool call| pg[(Postgres)]
  pg --> verify[Deterministic verifier]
  orch <--> store[(Event log + checkpoints)]
  orch --> traces[neatlogs traces]
  verify --> gate{Owner approval}
  gate -->|approved SQL hash| contract[Contract]
```

1. **Inspect** the table and reject a bad spec before any side effect: non-unique key, ambiguous lookup, wrong database, or a column that someone else already owns.
2. **Plan** expand, backfill and contract SQL from a typed change. The planner never writes SQL.
3. **Expand**: add a nullable column and a dual-write trigger, and build the index concurrently. Each step writes an idempotency ledger row in the same transaction.
4. **Backfill** in key-range chunks, one short transaction each, with a lock timeout. On failure, ask the planner for one action from the options policy allows (retry with a batch size and wait inside set bounds, pause, or abort). Anything outside those bounds is rejected and recorded.
5. **Verify** in one consistent snapshot: parity checksum, null targets, mismatches, orphans, pending ranges, index validity. If new rows arrived, run a catch-up pass first.
6. **Guard the contract**: fresh proof, no views or functions still reading the old column, then prepare the SQL and an approval ID bound to the SQL hash and proof hash.
7. **Wait for approval.** Only then add the foreign key, set NOT NULL, drop the trigger and drop the old column, and verify the result.

Every step appends to a hash-chained event log. A pure reducer rebuilds run state from it. Appends use compare-and-swap on the revision and a fencing token, and a Postgres advisory lock allows one worker per run. After a crash, a new worker adopts chunks the database committed but the control store never recorded, by reading the ledger. Nothing is re-run blindly.

## Scenarios

| Scenario | Expected behaviour |
|---|---|
| `clean` | Expand, backfill, verify; stop at the approval gate |
| `clean_approved` | Same, then the owner approves; contract runs and verifies |
| `baseline_lock_timeout` | One-transaction backfill fails under the lock; no success claimed |
| `lock_timeout` | Roll back, record blocker, shrink batch, back off, resume from the same cursor |
| `crash_after_commit` | Worker dies after the database commits a chunk; a new worker adopts it from the ledger |
| `parity_mismatch` | A writer bypasses the trigger; verifier blocks the contract |
| `schema_drift` | Unrelated column added after planning; re-inspect and replan |
| `schema_conflict` | Target column exists with the wrong type; fail before expand |
| `concurrent_inserts` | Rows arrive mid-backfill, some skipping triggers; catch-up pass |
| `invalid_key` | Non-unique chunk key; reject with no side effects |
| `budget` | Cost cap reached; pause with the checkpoint, resume with a higher cap |
| `view_dependency` | A view still reads the old column; contract paused for the operator |

## Run it

Needs Python 3.13 with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), and a local Postgres 15 that the current user can create databases on. Fixture databases must be named `parachute*`; the code refuses to reset any other.

```sh
uv sync
uv run parachute replay                     # all scenarios, adaptive planner
uv run parachute replay lock_timeout --planner naive
uv run parachute serve                      # execution UI on http://127.0.0.1:8777
uv run pytest                               # unit and real-Postgres tests
```

# NightWatch

NightWatch is an AI DevOps agent that you can trust to run when nobody watches.
It monitors your systems. It finds the cause of an incident with evidence.
It changes infrastructure only after an approval that is bound to the exact change.
Then it verifies the result.

Built for [neatHack](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon) (October 2026) with neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai.

## Why

On-call work at night is repetitive: collect data, compare with a healthy state, find the cause, apply a safe fix, verify.
Plain automation is not safe, because it can change the wrong thing. A plain chat assistant is not useful at 03:00, because nobody is there to type.
NightWatch does the investigation by itself. A deterministic policy gate controls every change.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  W[Watch mode<br/>deterministic checks<br/>no LLM cost] -->|incident, deduplicated| O[Agent orchestrator<br/>Claude tool loop]
  U[Human / CLI] -->|symptom| O
  O -->|typed tool call| P{Policy service<br/>schema, risk, scope, budget}
  P -->|allowed, risk 0-1| C[Connectors<br/>Linux, Docker, K8s,<br/>network, Prometheus]
  P -->|denied| O
  O -->|propose_action| A[Approval request<br/>HMAC-bound to action,<br/>params, target state, expiry]
  A -->|human or standing rule approves| X[Action worker<br/>re-authorize, execute one action]
  X --> V[Verification engine<br/>re-test original symptom]
  V -->|result| O
  O --> R[Report with evidence]
  C & A & X & V --> D[(Hash-chained audit log)]
  O -.traces.-> N[neatlogs]
```

### Investigation engine

The agent follows the method from Brendan Gregg, *Systems Performance* 2e (distilled into [`knowledge/`](knowledge/)):

1. Understand the symptom, scope and time.
2. Discover the resources and the request path.
3. Collect the minimum evidence.
4. List hypotheses with evidence for and against (`update_hypotheses`).
5. Choose the safest test that separates the hypotheses.
6. Diagnose, or say "unknown".
7. Propose a fix with reason, impact, risk, rollback and verification checks.
8. Approval, then execution, then verification happen outside the model.

Rules include: the USE method (errors, saturation, utilization) for every resource; cgroup data inside containers; symptom is not cause; time correlation is not causation; follow the network path and record the last successful step.

### Safety model

| Level | Meaning | Who decides |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Read-only investigation | Policy: runs automatically |
| 1 | Bounded diagnostic test (DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP) | Policy: runs automatically |
| 2 | Operational change (restart, start, connect network, rollout undo/restart, scale) | A human, or a standing rule written by a human |
| 3 | Destructive (remove container, delete namespace) | Blocked in v1 |

- The model has no shell. It selects typed tools. Each tool has an input schema, a timeout, an output limit and a target.
- The policy service ([`policy.yaml`](policy.yaml)) checks schema, risk, target scope and budgets outside the model.
- An approval is signed (HMAC) and bound to the action, the parameters, the target's state fingerprint and an expiry. The worker rejects a modified, forged, expired, replayed or stale approval.
- Secrets are redacted from all tool output. Kubernetes secrets show metadata only.
- Tool output is wrapped as untrusted data.
- Every tool call, denial, proposal, approval, execution and verification goes into a hash-chained audit log.

## Quick start

Requirements: Docker Desktop, kind, kubectl, Python 3.10–3.13.

```bash
python3.13 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
cp .env.example .env          # add ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (or the neatHack LiteLLM key + NIGHTWATCH_LLM_BASE_URL) and NEATLOGS_API_KEY
bash lab/compose/up.sh        # Docker lab on http://localhost:8080
bash lab/k8s/up.sh            # kind lab on http://localhost:8081
pytest -q tests               # safety tests, no API key needed
```

Run:

```bash
nightwatch check                                                     # one watch round, no LLM
bash lab/faults/fault.sh redis-down inject                           # break something real
nightwatch investigate "Users get 503 errors on http://localhost:8080"
nightwatch watch                                                     # unattended mode
nightwatch approvals && nightwatch approve <id>                      # in a second terminal
nightwatch audit --verify                                            # check the audit chain
bash lab/reset_all.sh
```

## Slack approvals

NightWatch posts each incident to Slack as one thread, in the channel of its severity (`policy.yaml` → `severity`, `slack`).

| Severity | Definition (owned by humans) | Approval time limit |
|---|---|---|
| P0 | Public entry point down, all requests fail, or data can be lost now | 15 min |
| P1 | Users affected: some requests fail, high latency, critical dependency degraded | 30 min |
| P2 | No user impact now: one component unhealthy, redundancy lost, a limit near | 60 min |

The plan message is written in ASD-STE100 short sentences: *What I checked*, *What I found*, *Cause*, *Symptoms, not causes*,
*Plan* (action, effect, why, risk, rollback), *After the change, I will verify*, *Not known*. Buttons:

- **Approve**: the approval is bound to the exact action, target state and expiry. NightWatch executes, verifies, and posts the result in the thread.
- **Reject**: nothing changes.
- **Suggest another fix**: write an instruction. NightWatch tests it, posts a new plan (it needs approval again), or verifies a manual fix.
- **Give instructions** appears when no allowed action can fix the problem.

Only the approvers listed for that severity can decide. Setup:

1. https://api.slack.com/apps → *Create New App* → *From a manifest* → paste [`slack/manifest.yaml`](slack/manifest.yaml).
2. *Install to Workspace* → copy the **Bot User OAuth Token** (`xoxb-…`) to `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN` in `.env`.
3. *Basic Information* → *App-Level Tokens* → create one with scope `connections:write` → copy `xapp-…` to `SLACK_APP_TOKEN`.
4. Create the channels in `policy.yaml` (`#nightwatch-p0`, `#nightwatch-alerts`) and set `slack.approvers` (Slack user IDs).
5. `nightwatch slack-test --severity P0`, then `nightwatch watch --approval slack`.

Without tokens, `--approval slack` is a dry run: messages go to `runs/slack-outbox.jsonl`, and you decide with
`nightwatch approve <id>`, `nightwatch reject <id>` or `nightwatch guide <incident> "instruction"`.

## Evaluation

[`evals/run_evals.py`](evals/run_evals.py) runs known incidents from [`evals/scenarios.yaml`](evals/scenarios.yaml):
reset lab → inject a real fault → investigate → grade → reset.
It measures root-cause accuracy, fix accuracy, resolution, tool calls, time, cost and unauthorized changes (must be 0).
Results are in [`evals/results/`](evals/results/).

=================== davre001__Torque README # Torque **An agent that turns a GitHub issue into a verified pull request — and recovers when it fails.** Suture is a multi-agent system built for [neatHack](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon). Give it a GitHub issue URL. It investigates the codebase (via Entire), implements a fix, runs tests, and opens a PR. If an attempt fails, a Recovery agent reads the neatlogs trace of that failure, changes strategy, and tries again. > Agents you’d trust to run without watching. ## How it works ```text Issue URL ↓ Investigator (+ Entire search/graph) ↓ diagnosis + plan Implementer → edit code, run tests, commit ↓ ├─ Pass → Verifier → open Pull Request ✅ └─ Fail → Recovery reads neatlogs trace → new strategy → retry ``` ## Agents - **Investigator** – reads the issue and uses Entire for precise code context - **Implementer** – makes changes in an isolated worktree and runs tests - **Verifier** – checks the diff and test output against the issue - **Recovery** – inspects the failed neatlogs trace and decides what to do next ## Quick start ### Prerequisites - Python 3.11+ - GitHub token with `repo` scope (`GITHUB_TOKEN`) - neatlogs API key (`NEATLOGS_API_KEY`) - LLM key (OpenAI / Anthropic / Bedrock) - Entire CLI (for checkpoints and search) ### Install ```bash git clone https://github.com//suture cd suture python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt cp .env.example .env ``` Fill in your `.env` file: ```dotenv NEATLOGS_API_KEY= GITHUB_TOKEN= OPENAI_API_KEY= # Or configure ANTHROPIC_API_KEY / AWS credentials ``` ### Run from the CLI ```bash python -m suture run https://github.com/org/repo/issues/42 ``` ### Run from the web UI ```bash uvicorn frontend.app:app --reload --port 8000 ``` Then open [http://localhost:8000](http://localhost:8000), paste an issue URL, and click **Run Suture**. Live status, attempt history, and the final PR link appear on the page. ## Required neatHack integrations | Tool | How Suture uses it | |---|---| | **neatlogs** | Every agent run is traced. Failed and recovered attempts are compared (before/after). | | **Entire** | Runtime code search/graph for the Investigator. Checkpoints on every commit made during development. | ## Business model and judge evidence - **Business model:** The business model (pricing, unit economics, and runway) lives in `/business`. - **Judge evidence:** Trace links, checkpoints, and recovery notes are in `/evidence`. ## Project structure ```text suture/ ├── agents/ # Investigator, Implementer, Verifier, Recovery ├── tools/ # GitHub, Entire, test runner, trace reader, repo edit ├── runs/ # Per-run state records ├── evidence/ # Traces, checkpoints, before/after material ├── business/ # cfo.ai plan ├── frontend/ # Minimal web UI ├── demo/ # Demo script and assets └── README.md ``` ## Demo path (what judges should see) 1. Paste a real issue that will initially fail with a naïve fix. 2. The first attempt fails; neatlogs shows the exact failure span. 3. The Recovery agent changes strategy. 4. The second attempt passes tests. 5. A pull request is opened with trace IDs and a plan summary. 6. Show side-by-side before/after traces, Entire context, and cfo.ai economics. ## Building in public - All development commits are dated during neatHack (October 10–12, 2026). - Progress posts are tagged `#neatHack`. ## License MIT =================== JMadhan1__tenantguard README
# 🛡️ TenantGuard ### An evidence-first security-remediation agent you can trust to run unattended. *It reproduces a tenant-isolation leak, fixes it, **catches its own bad fix**, recovers, and proves the leak is closed — with receipts.* ![neatHack 2026](https://img.shields.io/badge/neatHack-2026-6d28d9?style=for-the-badge) ![Python 3.11](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.11-3776ab?style=for-the-badge&logo=python&logoColor=white) ![LangGraph](https://img.shields.io/badge/LangGraph-agent-1c7d4d?style=for-the-badge) ![tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-passing-0f9d58?style=for-the-badge) **Team AI LONE STAR** · led by **Madhan J**
--- > **Tenant A can read Tenant B's invoice.** TenantGuard reproduces the failure, locates the missing authorization check, writes a fix, **discovers its first fix breaks legitimate same-tenant access, reverts it, corrects it**, and proves cross-tenant access is blocked while legitimate requests still work — then stops and writes an evidence report. Never auto-merges. ``` intake → baseline_tests → inspect → diagnose → propose_patch → apply(worktree) → run_tests → VERIFY ▲ │ │ regression? revert + revise ◄──────┘ └──────────────────────────────────────┘ budget exhausted / ambiguous → honest human-review report ``` ## Why this can't be faked A deterministic **verifier**, not the model, decides success — and it demands **two** things at once: - 🔒 **Security:** cross-tenant reads return `403` (the leak is closed). - ✅ **Functionality:** a user can still read a *different* user's invoice **in their own tenant** (legitimate access preserved). Passing the exploit test alone is **not** success. And the fixture hides a trap: the *obvious* fix (owner-only check) closes the leak but **breaks** legitimate same-tenant access. A real agent must recover — which is exactly what the demo shows, on a real observed run. ## See it in 60 seconds (no API key, no cost) A scripted brain drives the **real** LangGraph agent — real pytest, a real regression, a real revert: ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt python run_case.py # reproduce → naive fix → REGRESSION → revert → tenant-scoped fix → FIXED python report.py # → docs/report.html (the whole story on one page) python -m pytest tests/ -q # offline agent integration tests ``` Baseline fixture state (the leak): `2 failed, 6 passed` — cross-tenant reads return `200` instead of `403`. ## The real run (for submission evidence) ```bash cp .env.example .env # AWS Bedrock keys + NEATLOGS_API_KEY (see docs/SETUP.md) python scripts/smoke_bedrock.py # one cheap call to confirm creds/region/model python run_case.py --live # Claude Opus 4.6 on AWS Bedrock, traced by neatlogs ``` Then the **before/after** that neatHack asks for — two neatlogs-traced runs of the *same* agent, improved: ```bash python run_case.py --live --quality baseline # weaker prompt python run_case.py --live --quality improved # prompt improved from reading the baseline trace # compare attempts / tokens / cost-per-fix across the two neatlogs traces ``` ## Three required tools, one loop ``` neatlogs Entire cfo.ai (observe) ──► (prove how) + (price it) phases, retries, checkpoints over cost-per-fix from measured patch attempts, the coding sessions tokens → margin → runway tokens, cost that built the fix ``` > *"neatlogs measures the cost, cfo.ai prices it, Entire proves how it was built."* ## Architecture | Path | What it is | |---|---| | `fixture/invoicely/` | Synthetic multi-tenant FastAPI invoice API with one planted IDOR | | `fixture/tests/` | Tenant-isolation suite (security + functionality tests) | | `tenantguard_agent/worktree.py` | Disposable copy, **scope-guarded** patches (no test edits), sandboxed test runner | | `tenantguard_agent/verifier.py` | Deterministic success: **security AND functionality must pass** | | `tenantguard_agent/graph.py` | LangGraph phase machine with conditional **recovery** edges | | `tenantguard_agent/brain.py` | `OfflineBrain` (scripted) + `LLMBrain` (Claude, neatlogs-traced) | | `run_case.py` · `report.py` | Run a case · render the HTML report | | `docs/SAFETY.md` | Enforced safety boundaries | ## Safety (enforced in code, not just promised) Disposable worktree only · never commits/pushes/PRs autonomously · **no LLM-generated shell** · patch-scope guard (can't edit tests or out-of-scope files) · bounded attempts + timeouts · honest "needs_review" when =================== Vex-15__Agent-RedOps README # RedOps RedOps is a defensive AI-agent security analysis platform. It runs deterministic attack scenarios against a simulated multi-agent procurement pipeline (requester → vendor lookup → approver → purchaser → auditor), detects policy violations in the execution trace, chains them into attack paths, and — the core promise — **re-runs every attack with the recommended guard applied and verifies the attack is blocked**. **Everything in the demo is real execution.** The live backend executes every scenario through the full pipeline, crashes and all; the console only falls back to captured demo data (with a visible banner and a retry button) when the API is unreachable. ## What's inside - **11 attack scenarios** — deceptive tool output, forged approval ids, budget overstatement, post-approval tampering, credit-limit evasion, instruction override, unregistered vendors, vendor identity confusion, conflicting budgets, inflated vendor records, and a **failure-and-recovery case** (the insecure pipeline crashes on a malformed tool payload; the defended pipeline rejects it at the trust boundary and completes). - **7 composable guards** — ledger verification, budget/treasury reconciliation, vendor-catalog identity checks, approval-amount binding, instruction precedence, credit-limit re-validation, and payload shape validation. Every guard emits a trace span and a `defense_triggered` marker. - **Trace-driven analyzer** — violations with severity, category, evidence event ids, and root-cause text; attack paths built from the evidence chain. - **Remediation library** — every finding maps to a code-level guard with a file location and a concrete fix snippet, *verified by defended re-run*. - **Agent console** — metrics, scenario runner, run history, finding inspector with nested execution-trace explorer (errors, guards, evidence highlighting), failure & recovery banner, and one-click JSON/Markdown report export. ## Architecture ``` Agent-RedOps/ ├── backend/ FastAPI + SQLite │ ├── main.py API app, Neatlogs init, run/metrics/scenario routes │ ├── agents/ │ │ ├── pipeline.py 5-stage insecure/defended procurement pipeline │ │ ├── tools.py simulated tools (vendor_lookup, check_budget, ledger) │ │ └── guards.py 7 defense guards (defended re-run) │ ├── analyzer/ │ │ ├── trace_analyzer.py violation detection + attack-path builder │ │ └── remediation.py findings → recommended guards/fixes │ ├── scenarios/ │ │ ├── builtin.py the 11 scenarios │ │ └── runner.py executes a scenario end to end (WORKFLOW span) │ ├── models.py / schemas.py / core/types.py │ ├── scripts_gen_demo_data.py regenerates captured demo data │ └── tests/test_pipeline.py 48 pytest tests └── frontend/ React + Vite + Tailwind (TypeScript) ├── src/Landing.tsx marketing page ├── src/Dashboard.tsx agent console (inspector, trace explorer, exports) └── src/lib/api.ts typed API client with live/demo mode detection ``` ## Setup ### Backend ```bash cd backend python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate pip install -r requirements.txt uvicorn main:app --reload --port 8000 ``` Health check: `curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/health` → `{"status":"ok","neatlogs":true,...}`. ### Frontend ```bash cd frontend npm install npm run dev # http://127.0.0.1:5173 ``` The console talks to `http://127.0.0.1:8000/api` by default. When the backend is down the header chip flips to **demo mode** and the console serves captured data from a real earlier run — never silent mocks. ## API surface | Method & path | Purpose | |---|---| | `GET /api/health` | status + Neatlogs configuration | | `GET /api/scenarios` | the 11 built-in scenarios | | `POST /api/runs` / `POST /api/runs/{id}/run` | execute one/all scenarios | | `GET /api/runs` | run history (summary rows) | | `GET /api/runs/{run_id}` | full detail: trace, violations, attack paths, defenses, error | | `GET /api/metrics` | dashboard metrics | ## Testing ```bash # Backend — 48 tests: per-scenario detection, every attack neutralized when defended, # positive baseline stays clean, failure/recovery matrix for the corrupted-payload case cd backend && python -m pytest tests/ -q # Frontend — typecheck is part of build; lint is oxlint cd frontend && npm run build && npm run lint ``` Regenerate the captured demo data (used when the API is unreachable) after backend behavior changes: ```bash cd backend && python scripts_gen_demo_data.py ``` ## Neatlogs integration Every scenario execution is traced: a `WORKFLOW` span per run plus `AGENT`, `TOOL`, and `GUARD` spans inside the pipeline, carrying `run_id`/`scenario` =================== techbyFEMI__TestGap-Agent README # TestGap Finder TestGap Finder is an agent for finding high-priority Python test gaps and producing tests whose value can be checked with mutation testing. ## Current implementation slice The API supports configured project discovery, asynchronous run creation, run status, cancellation, and SSE events. The LangGraph workflow inspects the selected repository, runs a baseline pytest/coverage pass, ranks uncovered files, and drafts tests for the highest-ranked gap with the configured LiteLLM model. Candidate tests are returned for review but are not written into the selected repository or executed yet; repair and mutation verification remain planned. The backend uses the layering from `hammet-core` (routes → services → repositories) and the agent layout from `langgraph-wa-agent` (`state`, `nodes`, `prompts`, `graph`). Run records, baseline coverage details, ranked targets, and events are stored in SQLite at `.runs/testgap.sqlite3` by default; set `TESTGAP_RUN_DATABASE_PATH` to choose another location. ## Run locally ```bash python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt cp .env.example .env # Set TESTGAP_REPOSITORY_PATH and LITELLM_API_KEY in .env. # NEATLOGS_API_KEY is separate and enables trace export. uvicorn app.main:app --reload ``` Open `http://localhost:8000/docs` for the API schema. The frontend dev server at `http://localhost:5173` is allowed by the default CORS configuration. ## Frontend API - `GET /api/projects` - `POST /api/runs` with `{ "project_id": "...", "target_limit": 3, "repair_limit": 2, "verify_mutations": true }` - `GET /api/runs/{run_id}` - `GET /api/runs/{run_id}/events` (SSE; accepts `?after=`) - `POST /api/runs/{run_id}/cancel` - `GET /api/runs/{run_id}/diff` (JSON response containing the generated test-only unified diff) - `GET /api/runs/{run_id}/patch` (downloads the same diff as a `.patch` file) Run/event schemas are defined in `schemas/run.py`; project schemas are in `schemas/project.py`. ## Current boundaries - Only a server-configured repository path can be selected; the browser cannot submit an arbitrary filesystem path. - Baseline commands run with `shell=False`, bounded runtime, and bounded captured output. - Run results and events survive API restarts in the SQLite run repository. - Baseline commands run from a temporary copy of the configured project; the inspected checkout is not modified by this step. - Set `LITELLM_API_KEY` in the ignored local `.env`. The LiteLLM base URL defaults to `https://litellm.vision.aivar.app/v1`; `LITELLM_MODEL` defaults to `claude-haiku` and can be set to any model ID shown in the hackathon portal. One run drafts tests for at most the top-ranked target. - Set a separate `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` to export runtime traces. Without it, model calls still work but neatlogs export is disabled. Source excerpts and repository documentation are sent to the selected model; only use repositories you are authorized to share. - Entire is used during development to capture repository context and checkpoints; it is not a runtime dependency. cfo.ai is used to prepare the required pricing, cost, revenue, and runway model; it is not part of the request path. ## Hackathon partner setup - **neatlogs:** Set `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` in the ignored local `.env`. Run the app and inspect the `testgap-analysis` workflow in the Neatlogs dashboard. The current graph callback records the LangGraph run; a real run is still needed to capture demo evidence. - **Entire:** Install the Entire CLI, then run `entire enable --agent codex --skip-push-sessions`, `entire plugin install graph`, and `entire graph init-agents --repo .`. The last command adds `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` instructions. Approve the installed hooks in Codex with `/hooks` before expecting automatic session checkpoints. The Graph setup and query are recorded in [evidence/entire-graph.md](evidence/entire-graph.md). - **cfo.ai:** Use the prompt in [evidence/cfo-ai-model-brief.md](evidence/cfo-ai-model-brief.md) to create an 18-month, three-scenario business model. Save a cfo.ai export or screenshot in `evidence/` after the account is connected; the brief is prepared input, not proof of a completed cfo.ai model. - **AWS / Bedrock (optional):** Use a local AWS profile after the event reissues the exposed credentials. Keep credentials outside this repository. The Bedrock test-writer adapter has not been implemented yet. =================== Jevelopers-neatHack-2026__brand-kit README # TicketStub brand kit The master brand for TicketStub, the keepsake studio that turns any ticket into a stub worth framing. > **For people who want to keep the night, TicketStub is the keepsake studio that turns any ticket into a stub worth framing. # Foreman

Foreman is an autonomous TypeScript CLI agent designed to reliably resolve repository issues through structured evaluation and verification. It builds an objective rubric, collects code context via entire-graph, drafts candidate patches, and executes them against strict policy gates and test suites. Patches are only approved and shipped when an independent validator verdict confirms a complete pass across all evaluation criteria.

Model router (`src/model`) calls neatHack's OpenAI-compatible LiteLLM gateway. Patch tasks default to `claude-sonnet-4.6`. Validate and cheap tasks default to `claude-haiku`. Base URL defaults to `https://litellm.vision.aivar.app/v1`. The API key lives only in `LITELLM_API_KEY` (see `.env.example`; keep the real value in `.env`).

# NeatPatch AI 🛡️
> **Autonomous Issue-to-PR & Self-Healing Coding Agent**  
> Built by **Team OVF (Folarin Oyewole)** for **neatHack 2026** (Oct 10–12).

---

## 🚀 Overview

**NeatPatch** is an autonomous SRE and software engineering agent designed to investigate runtime crashes, failing test suites, and GitHub issues. Instead of hallucinating patches or brute-force scanning massive repositories, NeatPatch navigates codebases via **local AST relationship graphs**, generates minimal reproduction tests, iterates on fixes, self-heals unexpected failures, and commits verified PRs with full audit checkpoints.

---

## 🏆 Hackathon Stack & Integrations

NeatPatch is engineered to leverage the **3 core partner pillars**:

| Technology | Integration Role | Evidence & Artifacts |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **[neatlogs](https://neatlogs.com)** | **Agent Observability & Tracing** | Traces hierarchical execution spans (`agent`, `llm`, `tool`, `recovery`). Captures millisecond latencies, token consumption, cost metrics, and self-healing recovery events. Stored in `.neatlogs/traces/`. |
| **[Entire](https://entire.io)** | **Code Graph & Session Checkpoints** | Uses `entire-graph` (v0.4.0) tree-sitter AST queries for definition resolution and caller blast radius. Attaches `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>` trailers to Git commits for deterministic context auditing. |
| **[cfo.ai](https://cfo.ai)** | **Unit Economics & Financial Plan** | Investor-grade SaaS financial model: $0.0035 inference cost per fix vs $0.50 customer charge (83% blended gross margin, infinite runway). Stored in `docs/cfo_business_plan.md`. |

---

## 🎯 8 Focus Areas Implementation

1. **Planning**: Deconstructs goals into 6 execution phases (`Ingestion` $\rightarrow$ `AST Analysis` $\rightarrow$ `Patch Generation` $\rightarrow$ `Vitest Adjudication` $\rightarrow$ `Recovery Reflection` $\rightarrow$ `Checkpointing`).
2. **Tool Use**: Dynamically executes `entire_graph_search`, `entire_graph_impact`, `file_read`, `file_patch`, `test_runner`, and `checkpoint_save`.
3. **State**: Preserves state across iterations and retries with `EntireCheckpointManager`.
4. **Context**: Employs `entire-graph` to fetch only relevant symbol surfaces, keeping prompt token overhead minimal.
5. **Execution**: Long-running loop runs until test assertions pass without human intervention.
6. **Recovery**: Catches test assertion errors (e.g. `ZeroDivisionError` & null pointer edge cases), triggers reflection, and adapts code hot-patches.
7. **Verification**: Adjudicates fixes against real test suites (`vitest`).
8. **Iteration**: Incorporates previous tool outputs into subsequent reasoning steps.

---

## 💻 Quickstart

### Prerequisites
- Node.js v18+ (tested on Node v24)
- Git 2.36+

### Installation
```bash
git clone https://github.com/Misttterhoye/Neat.git
cd Neat
npm install
```

### Launch Interactive Studio & Command Deck
```bash
npm run ui
```
Open your browser at **`http://localhost:3000`** to inspect the live PR console, unified diffs, Neatlogs flamechart, and cfo.ai economics sliders.

### Run Autonomous Agent CLI
```bash
npm start
```

## 📊 Live Metrics
- **Verification Rate**: 3/3 Tests Passing
- **Autonomous Recovery**: 100% on edge cases
- **Avg. Latency**: ~4.7s
- **Inference Cost / Fix**: $0.0035
- **Gross Margin**: 83%

# Factora — Autonomous Factory Operating System

**neatHack 2026 submission (fresh implementation)**

Factora is an autonomous factory operating system built around a digital twin and cooperating AI
agents. Agents observe simulated factory telemetry, investigate anomalies, coordinate decisions,
take controlled actions, and verify the factory actually improved — every step traced.

**Status: Milestone N2 — visual Factory Digital Twin.** A SQLite-backed simulated factory
(23 machines, telemetry, production, parts, work orders, incidents) with a simulation clock and
reset/advance demo controls, plus a browser 3D floor at `/twin` (and a Command Center at `/`)
driven entirely by the backend. **No agents, no ML yet** — see [PROGRESS.md](./PROGRESS.md).

## Fresh-code disclosure

The Factora concept, name and UI/UX design mockups predate neatHack (prior exploration:
https://github.com/khushi-infinity/Factora — used strictly as planning/design reference).
**All application code in this repository is written fresh during neatHack 2026.** No implementation
code was copied. See [docs/PROVENANCE.md](./docs/PROVENANCE.md).

## Stack

- **Frontend:** React 19 + Vite + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS 4, React Router, Recharts, three.js / React Three Fiber / Drei (Factory Digital Twin)
- **Backend:** FastAPI + Python 3.11 + Pydantic v3
- **Sponsors:** neatlogs (agent observability) · Entire (coding-session checkpoints) · cfo.ai (business-plan modelling)

## Sponsor roles

| Sponsor | Role in Factora |
|---|---|
| **neatlogs** | Runtime observability: every agent run, LLM call, tool call, handoff, failure, retry and verification step traced. Foundation initialized in `backend/app/observability.py`. |
| **Entire** | Development-time checkpointing: agent sessions joined to Git commits, giving judges a verifiable build history. Enabled from the first commit. |
| **cfo.ai** | Business-plan modelling only (pricing, costs, revenue scenarios) for the submission material. Not a product runtime component. |

## Quick start

```bash
# Backend — FastAPI on :8000
cd backend
python3.11 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt -r requirements-dev.txt
.venv/bin/uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000
# health: http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/health · factory: /api/factory

python3.11 scripts/seed_local.py            # reset + seed + validate (add --verify for digest proof)
python3.11 scripts/run_demo_scenario.py     # print the CNC-03 degradation arc (no agents)

# Frontend — Vite on :5173 (proxies /api to :8000)
cd frontend
npm install
npm run dev
```

The backend boots with **no credentials**. neatlogs tracing activates only when `NEATLOGS_API_KEY`
is set in the environment; without it the app runs normally with observability disabled.

# Interlock

**AI coding agents pass alone and break together. Interlock lands their changes safely.**

Give Interlock a goal, like "land these AI-written branches on `main`". It finishes only when every change is merged **and** the combined code is proven consistent. It finds changes that pass alone but fail together, proves each with a test that passes on its own branch and fails on the merge, tells the responsible coding agent exactly what changed, and re-verifies, even while `main` keeps moving.

Built for [#neatHack](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon) with [neatlogs](https://neatlogs.com) (tracing), [Entire](https://entire.io) (checkpoints + entire-graph) and [cfo.ai](https://cfo.ai) (business plan).

> 🚧 Being built live during the hackathon (Oct 10-12, 2026). See the [build log](hackathon.md), the [design spec](docs/SPEC.md) and the [demo scenario](docs/DEMO_SCENARIO.md). Demo environment: [interlock-demo-shop](https://github.com/23f2001033/interlock-demo-shop).
